name: Maya Alvarez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for joining me, Maya. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers or government. Everything you say is confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior doctor at Northbridge Family Practice, a big clinic in a commuter town that keeps growing. Days are face-to-face appointments, and two evenings a week I do video consultations from home for the clinic, which is mostly rashes, coughs and repeat prescriptions. I use AI every day: one tool listens and writes my notes, and I ask another to explain guidelines I've forgotten.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like fixing things with my hands, honestly, like draining an abscess or injecting a stiff shoulder. I play five-a-side football on Thursdays, and I'd love to end up in sports medicine. What wears me out is the video evenings, staring at a screen until ten, typing up the same advice about fluids and rest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ha. That would be a funny ending to all the noise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the tools are still worth using, even if they didn't change the world. I'd probably post a little video showing how the note-taker saves me an hour a day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be fine. The clinic is growing, my pay is normal for a junior, and Tomás, my partner, has a steady job testing software at a payments firm. We've got about four months saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the AI tools and keep the video evenings, because they pay well. I'd sign up for a weekend course in joint injections next spring, for the sports medicine plan. And we'd keep putting money aside for a wedding in 2028.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Slightly disappointed, because I like new toys.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything about money on your mind right now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our rent went up a hundred and fifty last month, which stung. But we both earn, and we don't have a car loan. I'd call it fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Tomás say about this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner Tomás would be relieved, because he's been reading every week about software that tests software. In this world his job stays the same, and he'd tease me for getting excited about AI for nothing.

I'd post a short video on how the **note-taker** saves an hour a day.
think: I'd be **fine**: a growing clinic, normal pay and four months saved.
My partner's **software testing** job would stay steady.
do: Keep using **AI tools** and the paid **video evenings**.
Take a weekend course in **joint injections** next spring.
feel: **Calm**, and slightly **disappointed**, because I like new toys.
S0.quote: My partner Tomás would be relieved, because he's been reading every week about software that tests software.
fieldNote: Both incomes feel **secure** in this picture.
She'd miss the change, as an **early adopter** would.
Her pull towards **hands-on** sports medicine is already there.
A rent rise is the only **pressure**, and she shrugs it off.

steps.text: Keep doing two paid video evenings a week
Keep using the AI note-taker in every consultation
Take a weekend joint injection course next spring
Save each month towards the 2028 wedding

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Here's the card. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one feels very real. Half of it is already happening at Tomás's firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a chance for clinics to give patients longer appointments, if managers don't just cut staff. I'd post about it, and I'd be honest that I use these tools every day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the video evenings are exactly the kind of thinking work that goes first. A chatbot could handle half those rashes and repeat prescriptions. That's three hundred a week of my pay. And Tomás's job is literally checking code, which is on that list twice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move my extra hours from video evenings to minor surgery clinics, where I need my hands. I'd book the joint injection course this year instead of next. And I'd help Tomás update his CV and look at jobs testing medical software, where people still need to sign things off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a plan. The plan is the bit that helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which worries you more, your evenings or Tomás's job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomás's job, by a long way. I'd lose some extra money; he could lose his whole salary, and we'd be paying rent on mine alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change the wedding plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a smaller wedding. My mum would be upset, but I'd rather have savings than a big party.

steps.text: Swap video evenings for minor surgery clinics

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Here's the card. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's before our wedding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need income support for people whose jobs vanish overnight, and strict checks on AI in medicine. I'd still say I use AI, because pretending otherwise would be silly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be scared for us. Tomás's job would go in 2028, almost certainly, and most of my thinking work would go with it. The hands-on side, injections and procedures, gives me until about 2031, and that's not long enough to finish sports medicine training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Northbridge for every procedure clinic going, starting this month. We'd cancel the wedding venue and get our deposit back while we still can. And I'd ask my parents if we could move in with them for a year if Tomás loses his job, to save the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, and a bit angry that there's no time to do the sensible thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Tomás when the news came?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we're a team, and that I've got hands for three more years while he figures it out. Then I'd probably cry in the car on the way to work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Moving in with your parents, how would that be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Crowded. My dad snores, and my mum would reorganise our cupboards. But my parents' spare room would save us eleven hundred a month, and that buys time.

say: I'd call for **income support** and strict **checks** on medical AI.
I'd still admit I **use AI**, because pretending otherwise would be silly.
think: My partner's job would go in **2028**, almost certainly.
**Hands-on** work only lasts until about 2031, too short for sports medicine training.

fieldNote: She expects her partner to lose his **whole income** fast.
Her adaptability shows in **quick, concrete** moves.
She'd lean on **family** without embarrassment.
The **three-year** robot gap is her lifeline, and she knows it's short.

steps.text: Ask Northbridge for every procedure clinic going this month
Cancel the wedding venue and recover the deposit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Here's the card. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Better. Not easy, but better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to retrain people properly if governments start now. I'd post about which medical jobs need hands and which don't, because people ask me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I could get a sports medicine post before 2031 if I move fast. The thinking side of family medicine would go in 2031, but injections and joint work would last until about 2034. Tomás would have time to move into something new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply for the sports medicine diploma next year and do it part-time while working. I'd keep using every AI tool, so I'm the doctor who knows how to work with them. And Tomás would start a part-time course in electrical work, which he's always fancied.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a getting-on-with-it way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Electrical work? From software testing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner Tomás rewired his dad's shed last summer and loved it. Hands-on trades get the extra three years too, and maybe more, because every house is different.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the wedding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd keep it, but small, in 2028. Five years is enough to have a party first.

think: I could reach a **sports medicine** post before 2031 if I move fast.

fieldNote: The extra time lets her **specialise** in hands-on medicine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Here's the card. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the version where we can actually plan. I'd talk about it at work as a training question, not a panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be fairly relaxed. I'd have years in sports medicine by 2036, and the hands-on work would carry me to around 2039. Tomás could change careers without rushing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish family medicine, then do sports medicine properly. We'd have the wedding as planned. I'd put a small amount every month into an index fund, which is a cheap share fund, because if AI makes companies rich I'd like a slice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a little. Mostly I feel lucky to be young.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Lucky to be young, why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'd have time to change twice if I needed to. The doctors I'd worry about are the fifty-year-olds who've only ever done one thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you have children in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, around 2030. Ten years' warning means I wouldn't feel I was bringing them into chaos.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because Tomás and I would both be hit before we'd had a chance to move. What would help is income support while people retrain, and fast-track training into hands-on jobs, including for doctors.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what I'd keep. I'd keep my patients' hands in mine. A machine can read an X-ray, but I'm the one who can feel a shoulder click.

headlineQuote: A machine can read an X-ray, but I'm the one who can feel a shoulder click.
portrait: A **27-year-old** junior doctor at a growing commuter-town clinic who uses **AI daily**.
She lives with her partner, a **software tester**, whose job is the household's biggest risk.
She splits her work clearly into **screen work** and **hands-on** work.
Fast AGI **alarms** her; with more time she'd move into **sports medicine**.
She acts early and leans on **family** when needed.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because both she and her partner would be hit before they could **move**.
whatWouldHelp: **Fast-track training** into hands-on jobs, including for doctors.
